question: MCI vs cognitively normal detection from speech in older adults; same pair as C-71 (P-58 x P-6). The record's claim_b still names P-11, a duplicate of P-6; the 85.16% is P-6's figure.
metric: Accuracy with accuracy and AUC with AUC; the recorded P-58 '67-92%' is a multi-metric, multi-subset range, not one estimate.

figures.P-58: English cohort (14 MCI/19 HC), all features, LOO-CV: 84.8% = 28/33, Wilson 69.1-93.3%; AUC 0.932, Hanley-McNeil (14/19) -> 0.834-1.0. Hungarian cohort (13/20): 75.8% = 25/33, Wilson 59.0-87.2%; AUC 0.727 -> 0.543-0.911.

matched_figure_check: As for C-71: P-58's English cohort is P-6's population subset; accuracy 84.8% vs 85.16% and AUC 0.932 vs 0.8475 each lie inside the other's interval. The matched figures agree.
reason: This record duplicates C-71 since paper_b was repointed from P-11 to P-6. The recorded 85.16% falls inside P-58's recorded range, and on the matched English-speaking subset the two papers agree within uncertainty on accuracy and AUC. The verdict follows C-71.

quotes.quote: Besides an accuracy score of 84.8%, the recall/sensitivity and speciﬁcity values were also around 85%.
the framework achieves an overall accuracy of 85.16% and an AUC of 84.75%, with the corresponding std of 5.76 and 5.97, respectively.
Among the 68 randomized individuals, 34 were identified with MCI, while 34 were diagnosed with NC conditions.
